replying_to: Replying to IO-Adam: Rethinking Memory-Efficient Adaptive Optimizers from Gradient Computation
display_title: Official Review of Submission11844 by Reviewer 3s2b

summary.value: The authors propose a memory-efficient variant of the popular Adam optimizer that exploits the structure of gradients computed through backpropagation. The proposed method uses a second-moment estimate that is lower bounded by the second-moment estimate of Adam. The authors show a regret bound for the proposed optimizer, patterned off the analysis of Adam. Empirical results on fine-tuning, pretraining, and vision tasks demonstrate a 30-40% reduction in memory usage while maintaining comparing performance to Adam. A generalization of the main method is also proposed and explored.

strengths.value:
1. To my knowledge, the proposed idea is novel and simple to understand, being well-motivated in the context of backpropagation.
2. The memory reduction is significant, even compared to similar work on memory-efficient Adam variants.
3. The generalization via Holder's inequality is quite interesting and promising. I found the intuition that $p<2$ should work better to be very insightful.

weaknesses.value:
1. The theoretical contribution is extremely limited, essentially consisting of only a straightforward extension of the analyses in [1, 2]. A regret bound is common in online learning or reinforcement learning contexts but not necessarily standard for modern optimizer papers. It would be helpful to provide e.g. objective value or gradient norm bounds in order to strengthen the theoretical value of this work.
2. Given the primarily empirical nature of the contributions, the experiments should be held to the same standards as other empirical papers on optimizers, e.g. [3, 4, 5]. In particular, no evaluation is provided for larger models (7B+ parameters), making it difficult to conclude that the proposed method is scalable.
3. It is hidden in the appendix that the proposed method takes ~7% more time per step on average than AdamW, and it is merely mentioned that this implementation could possibly be improved. This may or may not have a significant practical impact, but I would have like to see more discussion in the main text.

[1] Diederik P. Kingma, Jimmy Ba. Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization, ICLR 2015.
[2] Sashank J. Reddi, Satyen Kale, Sanjiv Kumar. On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond, ICLR 2018.
[3] Jiawei Zhao, Zhenyu Zhang, Beidi Chen, Zhangyang Wang, Anima Anandkumar, Yuandong Tian. GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection, ICML 2024.
[4] Qijun Luo, Hengxu Yu, Xiao Li. BAdam: A Memory Efficient Full Parameter Optimization Method for Large Language Models, NeurIPS 2024.
[5] Tianjin Huang, Ziquan Zhu, Gaojie Jin, Lu Liu, Zhangyang Wang, Shiwei Liu. SPAM: Spike-aware Adam with Momentum Reset for Stable LLM Training, ICLR 2025.

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer 3s2b, 

Thank you for your valuable feedback. We sincerely appreciate your time devoted to the reviewing process. The following is our response to each of your comment.

> W1: The theoretical contribution is extremely limited, essentially consisting of only a straightforward extension of the analyses in [1, 2]. A regret bound is common in online learning or reinforcement learning contexts but not necessarily standard for modern optimizer papers. It would be helpful to provide e.g. objective value or gradient norm bounds in order to strengthen the theoretical value of this work.

We appreciate the feedback on the theoretical contribution. We respectfully disagree that it is limited. The primary conceptual and theoretical innovation of this work is the novel insight that the second moment of a weight gradient can be factorized along its input and output dimensions, and that using these separate moments leads to an effective and memory-efficient optimizer from a brand new perspective. Therefore, the theoretical analyses in the paper mainly focus on analyzing the connection and difference between our proposed method and Adam. In Sec. 3.4.1, we show that the second moment estimation from our method is strictly larger than that in Adam. The larger second moment estimation leads to smaller update on parameters. Since most theoretical analyses rely on gradient norm bound hypothesis, most of the analyses on Adam could be adapted to our proposed IO-Adam. We provided the regret bound not because it is the only metric, but to demonstrate within a standard analysis framework that our method retains convergence guarantees comparable to Adam. 

We agree that exploring other bounds, such as gradient norms, is interesting and will include a discussion of these directions in the final version. If there are any specific analyses of your interest, we are willing to further discuss whether our proposed method also satisfy those bounds.

> W2: Given the primarily empirical nature of the contributions, the experiments should be held to the same standards as other empirical papers on optimizers, e.g. [3, 4, 5]. In particular, no evaluation is provided for larger models (7B+ parameters), making it difficult to conclude that the proposed method is scalable.

Yes, our paper is indeed an empirical paper, where our experiments are conducted following previous works like [3,4]. Our experiments covers the model size (up to 1B parameters) in the main experiments of previous methods [3,6]. Our method does not have any model scale related attribute that may affect our method. To directly address your concern, we are currently running experiments on a 7B parameter model and commit to providing these results before the final decision is made / in the camera-ready version. 

> W3: It is hidden in the appendix that the proposed method takes ~7% more time per step on average than AdamW, and it is merely mentioned that this implementation could possibly be improved. This may or may not have a significant practical impact, but I would have like to see more discussion in the main text.

Thank you for this suggestion. We agree that the time-memory trade-off deserves prominence. Currently, we place the time complexity anysis in Appendix C and mentioned it in the main text (line 416-417). We will move a discussion of this trade-off to the main text in the final version. 

Similar to previous memory efficient optimizers, our method introduces a time overhead, comparable to previous methods like Galore and AdamSNSM. The overhead mainly comes from tracking the input and output gradient and update the second moment estimation for the input and the output gradient, where we use a hook in Pytorch to achieve these process. It could be improved with more sophisticated implementation. We will add more discussion in the main text if this paper is accepted with one more page available. Thank you for the valuable suggestion.

> Q1: In Line 772, it is mentioned that the analysis requires an additional assumption that was pointed out by Reddi et al. Could you clarify how this assumption is satisfied for the proposed method?

For Adam, this assumption as introduced by Reddi et al. is satisfied by tracking the maximum second moment estimation during training and use the maximum second moment estimation to adjust gradient, which makes sure that the second moment estimation monotonically increases. The assumption from Reddi et al. can be satisfied in IO-Adam by an analogous mechanism. We could use the maximum second moment estimation for the input and output gradient to satisfy the assumption.

We hope our rebuttal can address your concerns, and we will keep polishing our paper. We look forward to your further feedback and we are more than happy to address any further comments.

[1] Diederik P. Kingma, Jimmy Ba. Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization, ICLR 2015. 

[2] Sashank J. Reddi, Satyen Kale, Sanjiv Kumar. On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond, ICLR 2018. 

[3] Jiawei Zhao, Zhenyu Zhang, Beidi Chen, Zhangyang Wang, Anima Anandkumar, Yuandong Tian. GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection, ICML 2024. 

[4] Qijun Luo, Hengxu Yu, Xiao Li. BAdam: A Memory Efficient Full Parameter Optimization Method for Large Language Models, NeurIPS 2024. 

[5] Tianjin Huang, Ziquan Zhu, Gaojie Jin, Lu Liu, Zhangyang Wang, Shiwei Liu. SPAM: Spike-aware Adam with Momentum Reset for Stable LLM Training, ICLR 2025.

[6] Thien Hang Nguyen and Huy Le Nguyen. Lean and mean adaptive optimization via subset-norm and subspace-momentum with convergence guarantees.

display_title: Official Review of Submission11844 by Reviewer Qe6v

summary.value:
The paper proposes IO-Adam, a “memory-efficient” variant of Adam that separately tracks the input activations $X$ and output gradients $
abla_Y \mathcal{L}$ for each linear layer instead of storing full-size moment estimates. They re-express the weight gradient $
abla_W \mathcal{L}=(
abla_Y \mathcal{L})X^T$ and construct the second-moment estimate from the outer product of exponential moving averages of $X^2$ and $(
abla_Y \mathcal{L})^2$, reducing memory costs.

strengths.value:
1. This paper introduces an explicit dual-buffer implementation that separately stores input and output gradients, which can slightly reduce memory usage in small-batch settings.

2. The presentation of this paper is good.

weaknesses.value:
1. The method fails to save memory when applied to attention layers, since both $\nabla_Y \mathcal{L}$ and $X$ are high-dimensional matrices rather than vectors. In this case, storing the input and output gradient buffers actually requires more memory than storing the weight gradients themselves. Moreover, in most large language models, attention layers constitute the majority of parameters and computation, making this limitation particularly critical. In addition, they works well only if the batch size is small.

2. If the method can only be applied to linear layers, it is unclear how the attention layers are handled in the LLaMA and GPT-2 experiments or how any memory savings are achieved in those cases.

3. The buffer for the first momentum stores the input and output gradients from the most recent $c$ batches, while the buffer for the second momentum maintains a “ring buffer” of size $b$. Consequently, the first momentum and the second momentum are computed over different batches, resulting in a mismatch between the two moment estimates.

4. The second momentum estimation can be highly biased, potentially far larger than the ground truth. There is no theoretical guarantee or mechanism to control this bias.

5. The modified bias correction term $(1-\beta_2^t)^2$ is introduced only because the authors multiply two EMAs. There is no theoretical analysis or empirical evidence supporting that this modification leads to unbiased or stable estimates.

6. The experiment results are not convincing. Although IO-Adam exhibits a large second-moment bias, it still outperforms AdamW in all reported cases. The authors attribute this improvement to larger learning rates, which is an unconvincing and insufficient explanation.

questions.value:
1. Please define the variables $m$ and $n$ in Table 1.

2. From Eq.2, the statement of “the rank of the weight gradient is equal to the batch size $bs$” is not right. The rank should be less and equal to batch size.

3. No experimental details are given for the first-moment buffer. Please clarify.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission11844 by Reviewer Qe6v

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer Qe6v, 

Thank you for your thoughtful review and valuable feedback. We address each of your comments in the following.

> W1: The method fails to save memory when applied to attention layers, since both $\nabla_{Y}X$ and X are high-dimensional matrices rather than vectors. In this case, storing the input and output gradient buffers actually requires more memory than storing the weight gradients themselves. Moreover, in most large language models, attention layers constitute the majority of parameters and computation, making this limitation particularly critical. In addition, they works well only if the batch size is small.

> W2: If the method can only be applied to linear layers, it is unclear how the attention layers are handled in the LLaMA and GPT-2 experiments or how any memory savings are achieved in those cases.

We respectfully disagree with this assessment. We would like to clarify that the main focus of this paper is on the reduction of the second moment estimation and does not store all the $\nabla_{Y}$ and $X$. What our method does is using the second moment estimation of $\nabla_{Y}$ and $X$ (which are vectors) to replace the second moment estimation of gradient $G = \nabla_{Y}^{\top} X$ (which is a matrix). 
Though for each batch, the number of $\nabla_{Y}$ and $X$ is up to sequence length times batch size, they are used to update the moment estimation. Therefore, our method is applicable for any linear operations that are equivalent to matrix multiplication, where attention layer is composed by linear layers and non-parametric attention mechanism.

While we briefly introduce and discuss the possibility of using buffering mechanism to further reduce memory usage (line 184-197), it is a possible way to reduce memory usage when batch size is small but not the main purpose of this paper.

Taking the opportunity, we want to further emphasize the motivation of our method. Adam, one of the most popular optimizers, uses second moment estimation of gradient to adaptively adjust learning rate (allocate larger learning rate to parameters that generally have smaller gradient). **While many previous works focus on decomposing the gradient to reduce the memory consumption of the moment estimation, we take the structure of gradient into account, such that weight gradients is the product of input and output gradient, and use the second moment estimation of input and output gradient to adjust learning rate, saving the memory usage.** The motivation is straight forward: parameters corresponding to smaller input and smaller output gradient recieve smaller gradient and therefore could use larger learning rate. 



> W3: The buffer for the first momentum stores the input and output gradients from the most recent 
 batches, while the buffer for the second momentum maintains a “ring buffer” of size 
. Consequently, the first momentum and the second momentum are computed over different batches, resulting in a mismatch between the two moment estimates.

We beg to differ that this would be an issue. Adam itself uses different exponential decay rates (β1=0.9, β2=0.99) for its first and second moments, meaning they are inherently computed over effectively different time horizons. Our method follows this established principle.

> W4: The second momentum estimation can be highly biased, potentially far larger than the ground truth. There is no theoretical guarantee or mechanism to control this bias.

We would like to address this problem from two perspectives:
* **In adjusting the learning rate, our proposed method could be viewed as normalizing the input and output gradient based on their second moment estimation prior to the weight gradient computation to reduce the memory usage.** There is no bias when it comes to the second moment estimate for the inputs and the output gradients.
* In mimicking the beahviour of Adam, there is indeed a difference, where the gradient from our method is strictly smaller than that from Adam, as we have analyzed in Sec. 3.4. It means our method can endure a larger learning rate than Adam. 

> W5: The modified bias correction term is introduced only because the authors multiply two EMAs. There is no theoretical analysis or empirical evidence supporting that this modification leads to unbiased or stable estimates.
 
We wish to clarify a misunderstanding. We do not modify the bias correction term. We maintain two separate, standard EMAs for the input and output gradients. The correction term for the product of these two EMAs is therefore the product of their individual standard correction terms. We do not introduce any modification, but use two vanilla EMAs for the second moment estimation for the input and output gradient.

The optimal learning rate for our method is generally larger than that for Adam, which is a result in seperately track the second moment estimation for input and output gradient (we provide analysis in Sec. 3.4). We would like to clarify that we do not attribute the improvement to larger learning rates. Using larger learning rate is simply because our proposed method adjusts the gradient in a different way.

We thank the reviewer for the careful review. As defined in line 135, we define $x\in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $y\in \mathbb{R}^n$, where $m$ and $n$ is the width of the input and output. We will add a clearer definition in the caption of Table 1.

We will modify the statement to be more rigurous.

> Q3: No experimental details are given for the first-moment buffer. Please clarify.

As mentioned in the experiment section (line 360, 368), we use fused first moment estimation[1] but not the first-moment buffer, where the gradient is released after updating the first moment estimation. display_title: Official Review of Submission11844 by Reviewer ohrE

summary.value: This paper proposes a memory-efficient variant of the Adam optimizer, called IO-Adam. Specifically, for the second-moment estimation in Adam, this paper tracks the input vector and the output gradient for each layer. Since these are smaller than the full weight matrix, this approach significantly reduces memory cost. Experiments show that the proposed method is more memory-efficient than Adam, achieving around 30% reduction in memory usage. The paper also demonstrates that this tracking scheme estimates the second moment as an upper bound of Adam’s original second-moment estimate.

strengths.value:
1) The paper studies an important challenge—the high memory cost of training large models using second-order moment estimates—and effectively reduces memory usage compared to the original Adam.
2) The motivation is clear, and the proposed method is reasonable. By separately tracking the input vector and output gradient, it efficiently estimates the momentum of weight gradients.
3) Theoretical analysis and experimental results are clearly presented. The proposed method successfully reduces memory usage and achieves comparable or better performance than related baselines.

weaknesses.value:
1) According to the paper, memory storage depends on the batch size, meaning different batch sizes may lead to very different memory usage (larger batches may cause higher memory consumption compared to baselines). It is important to conduct a study evaluating performance and memory usage versus batch size.
2) I have concerns that in standard batch training, the input distribution may change over time due to sampling bias. Since this method stores input vectors, for earlier layers of the network, such estimation may lead to large deviations as the input changes drastically. Could this cause unstable training in the early stages? Or is a larger batch size required to stabilize it?
3) Another potential weakness is training time. This method may take longer per iteration compared to related works. It would be better to include total training convergence time and comparisons with baselines. If training time is significantly slower, the method’s practical usefulness may be limited.
4) Minor parts:  
4.1) The paper mainly focuses on training affine blocks; it would be useful to expand the scope to 2D CNNs.  
4.2) The paper notes that the optimal learning rate of IO-Adam may be larger than that of Adam. It would be valuable to study the optimal learning rate in broader experiments and, if possible, suggest a scaling guideline (e.g., a factor like 1.5x) for practical application.

questions.value:
1) Could the authors conduct a study to evaluate performance and memory usage versus batch size?
2) Given that input distributions change during training, especially in earlier layers, could this cause instability? Would a larger batch size mitigate it?
3) What is the training time compared to baselines?
4) How is IO-Adam implemented for CNNs, and what is the performance impact?
5) Could the authors clarify how to determine or scale the learning rate?

Please see the [Weakness] section for more details.

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer ohrE, 

we sincerely appreciate your valuable feedback. The following is our response to each of your comments.

> W1: According to the paper, memory storage depends on the batch size, meaning different batch sizes may lead to very different memory usage (larger batches may cause higher memory consumption compared to baselines). It is important to conduct a study evaluating performance and memory usage versus batch size.

Thank you for this important suggestion. We would like to clarify that the memory consumption of optimizer states in IO-Adam is independent of the batch size, as it only depends on the model parameters and our pre-defined buffer size $r$. The batch size primarily affects the memory for activations, which is common to all optimizers. 

In our proposed method we use the second moment estimation of the input and output gradient to adapt learning rate. Generally, our method is similar to previous low rank decomposition methods such as Galore. The main difference between our method and previous methods is that we take the structure of gradient into account and seperately track the moment estimation of input and output gradient in a buffer. Therefore, the memory consumption is determined by the pre-defined buffer size. As shown in Table 4, we present results of different buffer size, where our method is robust to various buffer sizes.

> W2: I have concerns that in standard batch training, the input distribution may change over time due to sampling bias. Since this method stores input vectors, for earlier layers of the network, such estimation may lead to large deviations as the input changes drastically. Could this cause unstable training in the early stages? Or is a larger batch size required to stabilize it?

In our experiments, we follow the settings from previous work [1] and use a same batch size for every optimizer. We do not observe any unstable training in the early stages. Instead, as analyzed in Sec. 3.4, our method can use a larger learning rate.
Generally, larger batch size could be better for a more stable training. We will add an experiment on training a model with different batch size to determine the robustness of our method.


> W3: Another potential weakness is training time. This method may take longer per iteration compared to related works. It would be better to include total training convergence time and comparisons with baselines. If training time is significantly slower, the method’s practical usefulness may be limited.

> Q3: What is the training time compared to baselines?

Thank you for raising a good question. We provide experimental results on the runtime overhead in Appendix C. Our method introduces an approximately $6\%$ overhead when tracking the second moment estimation for the input and the output gradient, which is common for memory efficient optimizers [1, 2], since the moment estimation needs to be computed every time, trading time efficiency for memory efficiency. For implementation, we use hooks in PyTorch to track these values and update the buffer.


> Minor parts:
> 4.1) The paper mainly focuses on training affine blocks; it would be useful to expand the scope to 2D CNNs.

> Q4:How is IO-Adam implemented for CNNs, and what is the performance impact?

Convolution can always be transformed into matrix multiplication by algorithms like im2col. To do so, convolution kernels will be flattened to vectors and the input will be reorganized into a large matrix. Therefore, the core principle of IO-Adam (factorizing the second moment based on the input/output gradient of a operation) is directly applicable to convolutional layers via the im2col transformation. We are currently finalizing experiments with CNNs (e.g., ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10). We commit to including these results in the final version of the paper to comprehensively demonstrate the general applicability of our method.


> 4.2) The paper notes that the optimal learning rate of IO-Adam may be larger than that of Adam. It would be valuable to study the optimal learning rate in broader experiments and, if possible, suggest a scaling guideline (e.g., a factor like 1.5x) for practical application.

> Q5: Could the authors clarify how to determine or scale the learning rate?

Based on our empirical observations across multiple experiments, we found that IO-Adam often performs well with a learning rate that is 6x to 8x larger than the standard learning rate used for AdamW.

replying_to: Replying to Rebuttal for Reviewer ohrE (part1)

comment.value:
> Q1: Could the authors conduct a study to evaluate performance and memory usage versus batch size?

We conduct an experiment on Llama-60M model, training from scratch on C4 dataset. In the our submission, the experiments are conducted following [1] where the total batch size is set to $512$. When changed to $256$ and $1024$, we report the following result:

| batch size | AdamW   | IO-Adam |
| ---------- | ------- | ------- |
| 256        | 3.57813 | 3.5625  |
| 512        | 3.51563 | 3.5     |
| 1024       | 3.5875  | 3.5556  |

To use a same amount of data, the experiment of batch size 256 is trained for 10000 steps, the experiment of batch size 512 is trained for 5000 steps, and the experiment of batch size 1024 is trained for 2500 steps. It is not exactly the larger batch size the better, but our method achieves a consistant relative improvement comparing to AdamW.

> Q2: Given that input distributions change during training, especially in earlier layers, could this cause instability? Would a larger batch size mitigate it?

This is a insightful question. You are correct that input distributions to early layers change during training. However, similar to Adam, our method is designed to handle this through the use of Exponential Moving Averaging (EMA) for the second moments of both the input and output gradients. The EMA mechanism inherently smooths over these temporal distribution shifts, this is the primary reason why we did not observe training instability in any of our experiments. 

While a larger batch size can generally provide a more stable gradient estimate for any optimizer, our results with different batch sizes (shown above) indicate that IO-Adam does not have a special dependency on larger batches for stability. Standard techniques like learning rate warmup are sufficient.

We hope our rebuttal can address your concerns and thank you again for your valuable feedback. We are more than happy to address any further questions and comments

display_title: Official Review of Submission11844 by Reviewer VV1t

summary.value: This paper presents IO-Adam, a memory-efficient variant of Adam that redefines how second moments are stored and updated. Instead of maintaining a full per-parameter second-moment matrix, IO-Adam tracks moving averages of squared input activations and squared output gradients, reconstructing an approximate second moment from their outer product. This change significantly reduces optimizer memory use while keeping similar convergence guarantees. The authors also introduce a buffer mechanism to stabilize estimates and a Hölder-based generalization to control the tightness of the approximation. Experiments on NLP and vision tasks show that IO-Adam matches or slightly improves AdamW’s performance while cutting optimizer memory by about 30–40 percent.

strengths.value:
* **Novel and well-grounded idea.** The approach builds on the natural structure of gradient computation, offering a fresh and simple way to reduce memory without complex matrix factorization.
* **Solid theory.** The paper shows that IO-Adam’s second-moment estimate upper bounds Adam’s and proves a matching regret bound, giving the method theoretical credibility.
* **Comprehensive experiments.** Evaluations across GLUE, ViT, and large-scale LLaMA pretraining show consistent results with significant memory savings.
* **Flexibility and extensions.** The buffer mechanism and the Hölder variant make the framework adaptable and potentially useful in broader settings.
* **Clear practical value.** The optimizer delivers meaningful savings in large-scale training while preserving accuracy.

weaknesses.value:
* **Limited applicability.** The method only directly applies to linear layers. It is unclear how IO-Adam handles other parameter types such as convolutions, embeddings, or normalization layers. This limits general usability.
* **Unclear memory accounting.** The paper’s claims of 30–40 percent savings lack a complete breakdown including the cost of buffers, first moments, and parameters that might fall back to Adam.
* **Runtime overhead.** Tracking inputs and output gradients increases implementation complexity and can slow training. The paper does not quantify this overhead clearly.
* **Hyperparameter sensitivity.** The buffer size and Hölder exponent are new and sensitive settings. Their tuning rules are not well explained.
* **Limited statistical reporting.** Some performance gains appear small, with no standard deviation or multi-seed results to confirm significance.

questions.value:
1. How does IO-Adam handle non-linear or non-matrix parameters such as embeddings or normalization weights?
2. Could the authors provide a full accounting of memory, including buffers, first moments, and fallback parameters?
3. How much runtime overhead does IO-Adam introduce compared with AdamW in large-scale training?
4. Is there a practical heuristic for choosing buffer size or Hölder exponent across tasks?
5. Could this approach be extended to convolutional layers or combined with other low-rank or quantized optimizers?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission11844 by Reviewer VV1t

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer VV1t, 

We sincerely appreciate your valuable feedback. The following is our response to each of your comments.

> W1: Limited applicability. The method only directly applies to linear layers. It is unclear how IO-Adam handles other parameter types, such as convolutions, embeddings, or normalization layers. This limits general usability.

> Q1: How does IO-Adam handle non-linear or non-matrix parameters such as embeddings or normalization weights?

You are correct that our method is primarily designed for parameters that exhibit a matrix structure during computation, including linear and convolutional layers, which covers most of the calculation. For example, convolution can always be transformed into matrix multiplication (e.g., via the im2col algorithm).

For non-matrix parameters like embeddings and normalization layer weights, we fall back to standard Adam, as their second moment estimation are vectors.

> W2:Unclear memory accounting. The paper’s claims of 30–40 percent savings lack a complete breakdown, including the cost of buffers, first moments, and parameters that might fall back to Adam.

> Q2: Could the authors provide a full accounting of memory, including buffers, first moments, and fallback parameters?

The memory usage of our method is similar to previous memory-efficient optimizers that use vectors to replace the matrix of moment estimation. In Table 1, we summarize the connections and differences between our method and previous memory-efficient methods. We use the same memory accounting metric, and our method achieves memory reduction by converting the moment estimation in matrix form into vector form. 

For a 1B model with FP16, the weight takes up 1.9GB, the first moment estimation, second moment estimation and gradient each take up the same amount of memory. By using two small matrices (containing several vectors), the memory usage will approximately reduce to 0.17GB.

> W3: Runtime overhead. Tracking inputs and output gradients increases implementation complexity and can slow training. The paper does not quantify this overhead clearly.

> Q3: How much runtime overhead does IO-Adam introduce compared with AdamW in large-scale training?

As we analyzed in Appendix C and confirmed in experiments, IO-Adam introduces a 6% overhead per iteration compared to AdamW. This is due to additional computation for tracking input/output gradients and updating our low-rank buffers.
Generally, previous memory-efficient optimizers introduce overhead, since the moment estimation needs to be recomputed every time. We posit that this is a highly favorable trade-off between time and memory efficiency.

> W4: Hyperparameter sensitivity. The buffer size and Hölder exponent are new and sensitive settings. Their tuning rules are not well-explained.

> Q4: Is there a practical heuristic for choosing buffer size or Hölder exponent across tasks?

In the following, we provide clear heuristics for the hyperparameters:
* **Buffer size $r$**: The buffer size in our method is similar to the rank of previous low-rank relative methods. We recommend setting r based on the available memory budget. As shown in Table 4, our method is effective with a variant buffer size and is robust. 
* **Hölder exponent $p$**: This parameter is theoretically grounded and less sensitive. Most of our experiments are conducted with it set to the default value of $2$, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method. We did not find it necessary to tune $p$ extensively. It could be adjusted if the gradient dynamics are known to be highly non-uniform, but this is an advanced use case.


> W5: Limited statistical reporting. Some performance gains appear small, with no standard deviation or multi-seed results to confirm significance.

We follow previous works [1,2] to conduct our experiments, with a random seed set for reproduction. We will add more multi-seed results to further validate our method and update the results during the discussion promptly. Thank you for your valuable suggestion.

> Q5: Could this approach be extended to convolutional layers or combined with other low-rank or quantized optimizers?

Since convolution can be expressed as a linear matrix multiplication (via the im2col algorithm), our method can be applied to convolutional layers combined with the im2col algorithm. For other methods, such as quantization, our method is orthogonal to them and can be combined with other memory-saving techniques.

Thank you again for the valuable feedback. We hope our rebuttal can address your concerns, and we look forward to your further feedback. We are more than happy to address any further comments.

[1] Jiawei Zhao, Zhenyu Zhang, Beidi Chen, Zhangyang Wang, Anima Anandkumar, and Yuandong Tian. Galore: Memory-efficient llm training by gradient low-rank projection.

[2] Thien Hang Nguyen and Huy Le Nguyen. Lean and mean adaptive optimization via subset-norm and subspace-momentum with convergence guarantees.

summary.value:
This paper received 4 reviews initially. The reviewers (score/confidence) are: ``VV1t(6/3)``, ``ohrE(6/2)``, ``Qe6v(2/4)``, ``3s2b(2/4)``. 

Their major concerns:
- In terms of methodology:
  - The proposed method seems not easily applicable to attention layers, leading to higher memory consumption than Adam due to high-dimensional matrix operations (``Qe6v(2/4)``).
  - Theoretical contribution is limited ("extremely limited") to straightforward extensions of existing works (e.g., regret bound from Adam and variants), lacking really novel insights (``3s2b(2/4)``).
  - Modified bias correction term is introduced without theoretical analysis or empirical evidence to validate its effectiveness (``Qe6v(2/4)``).
  - Only directly applies to linear layers, with unclear handling of convolutions, embeddings, and normalization layers (``VV1t(6/3)``).
  
- In terms of experiments:
  - No evaluation on models with 7B+ parameters, failing to demonstrate scalability to real-world large language model training (``3s2b(2/4)``).
  - 30–40% memory savings claim lacks a complete breakdown, hard to verify its validity (``VV1t(6/3)``).
  - Small performance gains lack standard deviation or multi-run results to confirm statistical significance (``VV1t(6/3)``).
  - No systematic study on the relationship between batch size and memory usage/performance (``ohrE(6/2)``).
  
- In terms of presentation:
  - Variables in Table 1 are undefined, and a technical error exists in the rank statement of weight gradients (Eq.2) (``Qe6v(2/4)``).
  - From Eq.2, the statement of “the rank of the weight gradient is equal to the batch size ” is not right. The rank should be less and equal to batch size. (``Qe6v(2/4)``).

reviewer_concerns.value:
`Qe6v` was concerned with the applicability to layers in addition to linear layers. The authors' rebuttal clarified this by saying that their method can be applied to any layer that exhibits a matrix structure - including the attention layers. This should partly resolve the concerns. But the applicability to other layer types such as conv, embedding (raised by `VV1t`) remains a problem.

`3s2b` was concerned with the novelty and theoretical contributions. Besides, the method introduced extra time cost (7%). The authors clarified these in the rebuttal. However, the clarifications did not change these problems. Instead, they argue about how we should perceive these problems. 

Based on the discussions, I believe these two negative reviewers's concerns are probably outstanding still.
